full_judgment:
2. The crucial question is in the facts and circumstances of the case whether the excess land is retainable in view of section 20 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. The owners made an endeavour for a certificate under section 20(4) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act so that they could retain possession of the land beyond the prescribed limit for the purpose of large scale farming on co-operative basis. Such certificate was granted by the Revenue Officer but the Member, Board of Revenue cancelled the certificate in 1963. He took the view that the application of the Co-Operative Society was a mere camouflage to retain the excess land. The owners challenged the order of Board of Revenue by filing a Writ Petition being Writ Petition No. 168 of 1964. This petition was dismissed in January, 1966 and further appeal before the Supreme Court of Pakistan was also without any success. The owners then formed a Co-Operative Society and filed a title suit being T.S No. 441 of 1966 for permanent injunction to restrain the Government for interfering with their excess land and allotting the same to any other person. Their main contention was that on co-operative basis they have undertaken to do large scale farming. The Trial Court granted temporary injunction on 15.6.66. Thereafter an interesting episode took place Proforma defendant No. 4 Basanta Kumar Swarnakar died on 29.11.72. As his son was not substituted as an heir, the son filed an application under Order 1, rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure to be added as a party to the suit. This application was rejected by the learned Subordinate Judge on 22.6.74. Thereafter a revisional application was filed being Civil Revision No. 1110 of 1974. Curiously enough, in that revision which is still pending before the High Court Division all further proceedings of the main suit were stayed. It is inconceivable how in a proceeding under Order 1, rule 10 all further proceeding in the suit could be stayed. That was highly irregular but it seems nobody took the trouble of rectifying the wrong, not even the Government. Then came the Martial Law on 24th March, 1982. It appears the plaintiff himself filed an application in the High Court Division for an order of 'status quo' in order to restrain the Government from disturbing the plaintiff's possession of the suit land. This petition gave rise to Civil Rule No. 32(R) It is to be noted that the temporary injunction that was granted on 15th June, 1966 was still continuing The reasons for moving the High Court Division for a status quo order can only be understood in the light of M.L.O. No. 14 of 1980 which barred the jurisdiction of the Court for granting restrictive order under certain circumstances. It seems it was the preemptive step by the plaintiff himself for asking for a status quo order. This prayer for status quo order was rejected by the courts below and the High Court also took the view that in view of the provision of M.L.O. No. 14 such order could not be passed. 

 “(4B) Notwithstanding anything contained in sub-section (4) and (4A) or in sections 39, 43 and 44 or in any other law for the time being in force, the land held under a certificate granted under sub section (4) or (4A) , by the prescribed Revenue Authority shall absolutely vest in the Government on the date when the Government shall take a decision in favour of the certificate-holder on an application submitted by him for granting a lease on a long term. basis in respect of such land wherein the certificate holder gave up the claim of compensation that would have been assessed under section 39 for the purpose of formal acquisition of such land, and such land may be leased out under the second provision to sub- section (1) of section 81 to the Certificate-holder without charging any premium thereof, on such terms and conditions as may be set forth in the lease by the Government, by terminating the certificate." 

 8. Shahabuddin Ahmed J:- I agree on the judgment proposed to be delivered by my learned brother Badrul Haider Chowdhury J. I would however add the following words: Sub-section (4) of s. 20 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act is a proviso to sub-section (2) of this section which prohibits retention of land by an ex-rent receiver or a cultivating raiyat in excess of the prescribed limit. Sub-section (4) enables an ex-rent receiver or a raiyat to possess land in excess of the specified limit for a particular purpose, i.e. for large scale farming on co- operative basis only if a certificate is issued to this effect by the Revenue Officer. The certificate is however, subject to periodical revision by the Revenue Officer. The certificate does not confer upon the said rent-receiver/raiyat any title to the excess land, but it simply enables him to retain possession of and hold the excess land for tile aforesaid purpose. It is, therefore, the certificate which is the only basis for possession of the excess land. In this case, certificate granted by the Revenue Officer was cancelled by the highest authority in the hierarchy of Revenue Officer, namely the Member, Board of Revenue-cum-Commissioner of State Purchase. As soon as the certificate was cancelled the very foundation of the possession of the excess land was demolished. The order of cancellation was challenged in Writ Petition No. 168 of 1964 but the Writ Petition was dismissed and the order of cancellation of the certificate was maintained. An appeal against the said order of the High Court was dismissed by the Supreme Court which observed that the ex-rent receivers got no legal right to grant of a certificate under sub-section (41 of see 20) After this decision of the Supreme Court no suit for permanent injunction against the Government is maintainable whether it is filed by the ex-rent receivers directly or in the name of their co-operative Society.
